title: Biker's death 'good news' to ex-hostage: Hwy. 401 shooting victim took former police officer captive in '91
article: Ontario Provincial Police Const. Dan Brisson, who was wounded in a gunfight on Highway 401 Sunday, was not the first officer to take a bullet from career criminal and biker-gang associate Daniel Lamer.
Richard Frohlich was working at his desk at Transport Quebec in Montreal yesterday when the Citizen told him the details of the weekend shootout that left Const. Brisson wounded and Mr. Lamer dead.
In an instant, Mr. Frohlich's emotions flashed from celebration, to anger, then relief.

The retired Montreal police officer was held hostage in 1991 for 15 hours by the then 27-year-old Mr. Lamer, following a botched robbery attempt. Mr. Frohlich, a constable at the time, was later shot twice before jumping through an apartment window to escape and end the standoff.
Mr. Frohlich was not unhappy to hear Mr. Lamer's 20-year crime rampage had come to a fatal conclusion.
"I take that news with great pleasure," said Mr. Frohlich. "It's difficult to explain. It's not easy to talk about.
"Lamer? He was a thief. It's good news for me."
In May 1991, Const. Frohlich answered a robbery call at a pharmacy in east-end Montreal during evening rush hour.
The young officer arrived on scene and chased two suspects, one of them Mr. Lamer, into a tavern. Inside, the two suspects overpowered him, took his revolver from his holster and handcuffed him.
The two then dragged the officer out onto the street and threw him in the back seat of a stolen Chrysler.
A chase ensued and other officers shot out one of the car's tires, forcing the two suspects and their hostage to flee into a nearby duplex, taking resident Julien Soulard hostage as well.
A lengthy standoff ensued; the officer remained handcuffed while the other hostage had his hands bound. Outside, about 50 tactical officers and negotiators worked to save the hostages.

The next morning, Const. Frohlich managed to slip one wrist from the handcuffs. The officer jumped on one of the suspects and retrieved his gun, then went into the bathroom to confront an armed Mr. Lamer.
The officer emptied his revolver, wounding Mr. Lamer at least once in the chest, while Const. Frohlich took bullets in the left shoulder and right thigh.
Mr. Lamer ran from the bathroom, boasting: "The pig, I shot him twice."
The second hostage also suffered a gunshot wound to one hand, as some 30 shots were fired. Const. Frohlich, meanwhile, jumped through the window, shattering the glass.
The incident ended soon after, when the suspects surrendered.
Somehow, throughout the 15-hour ordeal, Mr. Frohlich said, he remained confident he and his fellow hostage would somehow escape.
"So many things go through your mind -- it's almost impossible to explain," said Mr. Frohlich.
"You think of your last minutes with your wife ... and with your son. You think of saying your last prayer.
"It was all very difficult to me. Some of it is too hard to relive. It's not even easy now to talk about it."
Mr. Lamer and his accomplice faced 23 charges, including attempted murder, kidnapping, unlawful confinement, robbery and various firearms offences.
Mr. Lamer, who was on parole at the time for other crimes, was convicted and sentenced to 22 more years in prison, but was released on day parole in November.
Following the harrowing incident, Mr. Frohlich spent two years on stress leave, then returned to work in the police department's criminal intelligence unit.
"Right after it, it was difficult to even sleep," he said. "I had nightmares."
Mr. Frohlich took early retirement in 1997 and now works in administration with Transport Quebec.
Though he had thought of the incident often, he was unaware of what had become of his captor.
"I had not heard of him," said Mr. Frohlich. "Not until this."
